cards.title: Three ways to talk about the past
cards.body: English and Spanish both have three main pasts: I ate, I was eating, I have eaten. The first you'll learn is 'I have eaten', built with the present of a 'have' verb.

cards.title: haber, not tener
cards.body: Tener is for possession (and tener que). For 'I have eaten / gone' Spanish uses haber (silent h). Haber is very irregular, but easy to remember from its two vowels, a and e.

cards.title: he = I have; hemos = we have
cards.body: He (silent h) is 'I have', formed like sé from saber. We is the plural of I, so add the we ending -mos: hemos.
cards.caveat: Verbs don't make plurals with -s; that's for nouns and adjectives.

cards.title: ha, han, has
cards.body: Full set: he, hemos (I, we) · ha, han, has (he/she/it/formal you, they, informal you).

cards.title: -ar → -ado
cards.body: For -ar verbs, drop -ar and add -ado. Put no in front of the haber form.

cards.title: Used more than in English
cards.body: Spanish uses this 'have' past even more than English, so it can often stand in for 'I spoke' or 'did you…?'.

cards.title: Little words go before haber
cards.body: Anticipado isn't a 'to' form, so lo must go before the changed verb (hemos).

cards.title: por = for (periods of time)
cards.body: As in por favor (please, 'for a favour'). 'For a long time' = 'for much time'.

examples.en: We've anticipated it for a long time.
examples.es: Lo hemos anticipado por mucho tiempo.

cards.title: Deconstruct before you speak
cards.body: Split the sentence into thoughts: she has (ha), taken (tomado), it (lo, before the changed verb). You can be sure and still be wrong; that's fine, but don't guess.

practice.en: We've anticipated it for a long time.
es: Lo hemos anticipado por mucho tiempo
practice.why: por mucho tiempo = for a long time.
